Let me know if this makes any sense. People's wages are not arbitrary, they are determined by two things, the amount of value they provide to a company and the levels of supply and demand for their labor. So if you force employers to pay people a higher wage, in many cases the wage will be more than the amount of value the low skilled person generates. This means the business is basically acting like a charity towards that worker and they will likely fire them. In the case that the worker is still producing more value than his wage, the employers margins will be reduced. In many areas of the economy, such as restaurants, margins are already quite thin, so further reducing them will cause some businesses out of business and again the worker will be out of a job. So while it is true that some people will benefit from higher wages, many will lose their jobs or never have the opportunity to get a job in the first place. This also disproportionately effects the young and minorities who tend to be less skilled. Also the point of these low skilled jobs isn't to be a career or to raise a family on, they should be used for people to gain work experience, learn how business works, learn to be valuable to an employer and to move up over time.

Maybe parts of this argument hold up in service jobs, if margins are actually thin (I'm skeptical of this, given the huge profits that the fast food industry generates). But certainly in goods-producing jobs, productivity has skyrocketed, and real wages have been stagnant for at least 30 years. Workers are making more and more money for their employers, but there is no pressure to raise wages due to a surplus of labor.

Setting immigration policy is one thing, but the feelings that inspire those actions can easily inspire much darker actions. If you're willing to say, "no you can't immigrate," you might soon be willing to say, "we let too ,any of you in, you have to leave, or if we let you stay, you get fewer rights."
